newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault truck unit sees breakeven later this year.
newsitem.headline: Renault truck unit sees breakeven later this year.

text.p: Renault's money-losing truck division expects to break even in the second half of 1997, its managing director said on Wednesday, cheering investors concerned about the unit's troubles.
"We expect to return to equilibrium in the second half of 1997," managing director Shemaya Levy told a news conference.
He reiterated group chairman Louis Schweitzer's recent forecast that the commercial vehicle subsidiary would show a loss for 1997 but said it would be significantly lower than last year's.
Renault shares closed up 4.37 percent at 148 francs. "That was very good news," one trader said, referring to the forecast of a smaller loss for 1997.
He said it was a good sign, technically, that the stock had broken above 144 francs. "That opens the way to 165 francs," he said. Renault was partly privatised at this price in late 1994.

Renault Vehicules Industriels, the world's fourth-largest truck company, reported a net loss of 791 million francs for 1996, contributing to Renault SA's 5.25 billion loss for the year reported last week.
Schweitzer predicted the car division's results, excluding exceptional charges, would also arrive at breakeven this year.

Renault V.I. was hit by falling sales in its main markets -- the United States, where it owns Mack Trucks, and Europe -- while its costs rose due to stricter environmental standards and the launch of the Premium truck line and new versions of its buses.
Its unit sales fell 14.8 percent to 64,561 buses and trucks.
Levy said Renault V.I.'s objective from this year was to reduce costs by five percent annually. He expected a recovery in French truck orders to 40,000 for 1997 from 36,000 last year.

Renault V.I. generates 40 percent of its activity in France and aims through its new products to boost its presence in Germany and northern Europe, where it competes against Scania, Mercedes and Volvo.
Mack Trucks, which made an operating profit last year of $29 million, is expected to remain profitable in 1997, he said.
Renault was in talks with other truck makers on ventures to produce components, including the new generation of motors for 2000-2001 to meet European norms.
Company officials said the group was also looking at joint production of transmissions and axles, and a project could be announced this year.
Renault said last March that it had signed an accord with German components maker MAN to develop parts and engines but the cooperative deal started showing cracks in the autumn.
Senior Vice President Elios Pascual said Renault was not discussing joint production of engines for 2000-2001 with MAN. But "for 2004-2005, maybe we could join with MAN", he said.
